NEW HIRE REPORTING — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Alex Lee · Acme Corp

ABOUT THIS NEW HIRE REPORTING INFORMATION SHEET
This New Hire Reporting — Information Sheet describes the federal and California legal framework requiring an employer to report a newly hired or rehired employee to a state new-hire reporting agency, in connection with Acme Corp's hiring of Jordan Alex Lee, whose first date of work is October 1, 2026. It summarizes selected requirements of the federal Personal Responsibility and Work Opportunity Reconciliation Act of 1996 (42 U.S.C. § 653a) and California's implementing statute, Unemployment Insurance Code § 1088.5: what counts as a reportable "new employee" or "rehire," the reporting deadline, the information a report must contain, and the statute's own reporting penalties. It also summarizes California's separate reporting duty for certain independent contractors, Unemployment Insurance Code § 1088.8.

This information sheet is not the new-hire report itself, does not submit any report to the California Employment Development Department or any other agency on Acme Corp's behalf, and does not determine whether Acme Corp's own reporting practices for Jordan Alex Lee are or are not compliant with California law.

THE FEDERAL NEW-HIRE REPORTING FRAMEWORK (PRWORA)
Federal law requires each state to establish an automated "State Directory of New Hires" containing information that employers report on each newly hired employee. Correspondingly, federal law requires each employer to furnish a report — containing the employee's name, address, and Social Security number, the date the employee first performed services for pay, and the employer's name, address, and federal identifying number — to the state directory for the state in which the employee works. This federal requirement, enacted as part of the Personal Responsibility and Work Opportunity Reconciliation Act of 1996, is the underlying framework beneath state new-hire reporting programs such as California's; it exists mainly to support child-support enforcement, by letting states and the federal government locate a parent's new employer quickly.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "each State shall establish an automated directory (to be known as the “State Directory of New Hires”) which shall contain information supplied in accordance with subsection (b) by employers on each newly hired employee."
  — 42 U.S.C. § 653a(a)(1)(A) (Cornell LII text), Requirement that each state establish a State Directory of New Hires (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/42/653a)
  "each employer shall furnish to the Directory of New Hires of the State in which a newly hired employee works, a report that contains the name, address, and social security number of the employee, the date services for remuneration were first performed by the employee, and the name and address of, and identifying number assigned under section 6109 of the Internal Revenue Code of 1986 to, the employer."
  — 42 U.S.C. § 653a(b)(1)(A) (Cornell LII text), Employer's duty to furnish the report to the state directory (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/42/653a)
  Known gap: This is federal law, used as evidence of what the federal government requires — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any specific employer's situation. This information sheet is informational only: it does not itself file a new-hire report with the California Employment Development Department or any other agency, and it does not itself fulfill any employer's reporting duty. Both citations below are to different paragraphs of the same statutory section, 42 U.S.C. § 653a — subsection (a)(1)(A) (the state's duty to establish a directory) and subsection (b)(1)(A) (the employer's duty to report into it) — and are treated as one source, not independent; this clause draws no conclusion from that shared section other than that they are two halves of a single directory-and-reporting structure. Separately, this clause describes only the general reporting rule; § 653a itself carves out exceptions (a multistate-employer election in (b)(1)(B), a federal-government-employer routing rule in (b)(1)(C), and a narrow intelligence/counterintelligence employee exclusion in (a)(2)(A)(ii)) that are not summarized here. Federal law leaves each state to set its own reporting deadline and civil penalty within federal outer limits; California's own choices on those points are addressed in separate clauses of this information sheet, not this one.

CALIFORNIA'S NEW HIRE REPORTING DUTY AND DEADLINE
California implements the federal new-hire reporting framework through Unemployment Insurance Code § 1088.5, which since July 1, 1998 has required every employer to file specified information on new employees with the Employment Development Department ("EDD"), in addition to the routine wage reports already required under § 1088. An employer must submit the required report within 20 days of hiring an employee it is required to report. An employer that transmits its reports magnetically or electronically is not held to that same report-by-report 20-day clock; instead, it may submit its reports in two monthly transmissions, spaced not less than 12 days and not more than 16 days apart — an alternative batched-reporting schedule, not simply a shorter or longer version of the 20-day deadline.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "In addition to information reported in accordance with Section 1088, effective July 1, 1998, each employer shall file, with the department, the information provided for in subdivision (b) on new employees."
  — Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1088.5(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Unemployment Insurance Code, the general new-employee filing duty (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=UIC&sectionNum=1088.5)
  "Employers shall submit a report as described in paragraph (4) within 20 days of hiring any employee whom the employer is required to report pursuant to this section."
  — Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1088.5(d)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California Unemployment Insurance Code, the 20-day reporting deadline (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=UIC&sectionNum=1088.5)
  "Notwithstanding subdivision (a), employers transmitting reports magnetically or electronically shall submit the report by two monthly transmissions not less than 12 days and not more than 16 days apart."
  — Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1088.5(d)(2) (California Legislative Information text), California Unemployment Insurance Code, the alternative schedule for electronic filers (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=UIC&sectionNum=1088.5)
  Known gap: This is California law, used as evidence of what California requires — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any specific employer's situation. This information sheet is informational only: it does not itself file a new-hire report with the California Employment Development Department or any other agency, and it does not itself fulfill any employer's reporting duty. All three citations below are to different subdivisions of the same statutory section, Unemployment Insurance Code § 1088.5 — subdivision (a) (the general filing duty), and subdivision (d), paragraphs (1) (the 20-day deadline) and (2) (the electronic-filer alternative) — and are treated as one source, not independent. This clause corrects a framing worth stating directly: the electronic-filer rule in (d)(2) is not a categorically "shorter" deadline than 20 days; it replaces the per-hire 20-day clock with a twice-monthly transmission schedule, which can in practice fall before or after 20 days from any given hire depending on when in the cycle the hire occurs. Section 1088.5(c) also exempts United States government employers, and limits reporting by state agencies for employees performing intelligence or counterintelligence functions in specified circumstances; those exemptions are not elaborated here.

WHAT COUNTS AS A REPORTABLE "NEW EMPLOYEE" OR "REHIRE"
For California new-hire reporting purposes, an employer must report the hiring of any employee who works in the state and to whom the employer anticipates paying wages. Separately, an employer must also report the hiring of any employee who previously worked for that same employer but had been separated from that prior employment for at least 60 consecutive days — a rehire. A employee's return after a break in service shorter than 60 consecutive days does not, on the statute's own terms, trigger this separate rehire-reporting duty. California's 60-consecutive-day rehire threshold matches the floor set by the federal statute underlying this program, which defines a "newly hired employee" the same way for federal new-hire-reporting purposes.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Each employer shall report the hiring of any employee who works in this state and to whom the employer anticipates paying wages, and also shall report the hiring of any employee who previously worked for the employer but had been separated from that prior employment for at least 60 consecutive days."
  — Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1088.5(b) (California Legislative Information text), California Unemployment Insurance Code, the new-employee and rehire definitions (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=UIC&sectionNum=1088.5)
  "The term “ newly hired employee ” means an employee who— (i) has not previously been employed by the employer ; or (ii) was previously employed by the employer but has been separated from such prior employment for at least 60 consecutive days."
  — 42 U.S.C. § 653a(a)(2)(C) (Cornell LII text), Federal definition of "newly hired employee," including the 60-day rehire threshold (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/42/653a)

This information sheet is informational only: it does not itself file a new-hire report with the California Employment Development Department or any other agency, and it does not itself fulfill any employer's reporting duty. The two citations below are to genuinely independent, separately numbered sources — California Unemployment Insurance Code § 1088.5(b) and federal 42 U.S.C. § 653a(a)(2)(C) — not subsections of a single section, so no same-source caveat applies; this clause notes only that the two definitions happen to converge on the same 60-day figure, not that either is derived from the other. Neither statute defines a minimum hours, wage amount, or duration-of-employment threshold for when a first-time hire itself becomes reportable; on the text reviewed, the reporting duty for a first-time hire turns only on working in the state and an anticipated wage payment, not on any minimum length of the job.

INFORMATION A NEW HIRE REPORT MUST CONTAIN
California law specifies what a new hire report must contain: (A) the employee's name, address, and Social Security number; (B) the employer's name, address, state employer identification number (if one has been issued), and the identifying number assigned to the employer under Internal Revenue Code § 6109 (its federal EIN); and (C) the first date the employee worked. An employer may satisfy this reporting duty by submitting a copy of the employee's completed Form W-4, a form the department itself provides, or any other hiring document already being transmitted — by first-class mail, magnetically, or electronically.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "The name, address, and social security number of the employees."
  — Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1088.5(d)(4)(A) (California Legislative Information text), California Unemployment Insurance Code, required employee information (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=UIC&sectionNum=1088.5)
  "The employer’s name, address, state employer identification number (if one has been issued), and identifying number assigned to the employer under Section 6109 of the Internal Revenue Code of 1986."
  — Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1088.5(d)(4)(B) (California Legislative Information text), California Unemployment Insurance Code, required employer information (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=UIC&sectionNum=1088.5)
  "The first date the employee worked."
  — Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1088.5(d)(4)(C) (California Legislative Information text), California Unemployment Insurance Code, the first-date-worked requirement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=UIC&sectionNum=1088.5)
  "Employers may report pursuant to this section by submitting a copy of the employee’s W-4 form, a form provided by the department, or any other hiring document transmitted by first-class mail, magnetically, or electronically."
  — Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1088.5(d)(5) (California Legislative Information text), California Unemployment Insurance Code, permitted reporting formats (W-4 or equivalent) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=UIC&sectionNum=1088.5)
  Known gap: This is California law, used as evidence of what California requires — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any specific employer's situation. This information sheet is informational only: it does not itself file a new-hire report with the California Employment Development Department or any other agency, and it does not itself fulfill any employer's reporting duty. All four citations below are to different paragraphs of the same statutory subdivision, Unemployment Insurance Code § 1088.5(d) — paragraph (4)'s subparagraphs (A), (B), and (C) (the three required content items) and paragraph (5) (the permitted reporting formats) — and are treated as one source, not independent. The statute's list of required content is exactly these three items; it does not separately require, for example, the employee's date of birth or job title as part of this report. This clause does not independently verify the current name or number of any specific EDD-provided reporting form (the statute itself does not name one), so no form name is stated here.

PENALTIES FOR FAILING TO REPORT
California law authorizes the Employment Development Department to assess a penalty of $24 for each failure to report the hiring of an employee as required and within the time required, unless the failure is due to good cause; the penalty rises to $490 if the failure results from a conspiracy between the employer and the employee not to supply the required report, or to supply a false or incomplete one. These amounts are not California's own invention set independent of federal law: the federal statute underlying this program caps what a state may set its new-hire-reporting civil penalty at — no more than $25 per failure, or $500 for a conspiracy — and California's own codified penalty amounts sit at or under that federal ceiling.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "For each failure to report the hiring of an employee, as required and within the time required by this section, unless the failure is due to good cause, the department may assess a penalty of twenty-four dollars ($24), or four hundred ninety dollars ($490) if the failure is the result of conspiracy between the employer and employee not to supply the required report or to supply a false or incomplete report."
  — Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1088.5(e) (California Legislative Information text), California Unemployment Insurance Code, the codified penalty amounts (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=UIC&sectionNum=1088.5)
  "The State shall have the option to set a State civil money penalty which shall not exceed— (1) $25 per failure to meet the requirements of this section with respect to a newly hired employee ; or (2) $500 if, under State law, the failure is the result of a conspiracy between the employer and the employee to not supply the required report or to supply a false or incomplete report."
  — 42 U.S.C. § 653a(d) (Cornell LII text), Federal statute, the ceiling on a state's new-hire-reporting civil penalty (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/42/653a)
  Known gap: This is California and federal law, used as evidence of what California and the federal government requires — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any specific employer's situation. This information sheet is informational only: it does not itself file a new-hire report with the California Employment Development Department or any other agency, and it does not itself fulfill any employer's reporting duty. The two citations below are to genuinely independent, separately numbered sources — California Unemployment Insurance Code § 1088.5(e) and federal 42 U.S.C. § 653a(d) — not subsections of a single section, so no same-source caveat applies. This clause states the penalty amounts as codified in the statutory text itself; it does not independently verify whether either figure has since been adjusted for inflation by regulation or administrative action outside the statute, and does not state that these are the only consequences an employer could face (for example, the statute is silent on any private right of action, and this clause takes no position on whether one might exist under some other law). "Good cause" is not defined in the statutory text reviewed.

SEPARATE REPORTING DUTY FOR CERTAIN INDEPENDENT CONTRACTORS
California law imposes a second, independent reporting duty distinct from the employee new-hire reporting duty described above: a "service-recipient" — defined to include an individual, corporation, association, or partnership doing business in the state — that makes or is required to make an information return to the IRS under Internal Revenue Code § 6041A for payments to a "service-provider" (an individual who is not its employee for California purposes) must also report specified information to the Employment Development Department. That duty is triggered within 20 days of the earlier of two events: the service-recipient's aggregate payments to that service-provider first reaching $600 in a calendar year, or the service-recipient entering into a contract or contracts with that service-provider providing for aggregate payments of $600 or more in a calendar year. The required report includes the service-provider's full name, address, and Social Security number, among other identifying information.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Effective January 1, 2001, any service-recipient, as defined in subdivision (b), who makes or is required to make a return to the Internal Revenue Service, in accordance with subdivision (a) of Section 6041A of the Internal Revenue Code (relating to payments made to a service-provider as compensation for services) shall file with the department information as required under subdivision (c)."
  — Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1088.8(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Unemployment Insurance Code, the independent-contractor reporting trigger (IRC § 6041A) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=UIC&sectionNum=1088.8)
  "“Service-provider” means an individual who is not an employee of the service-recipient for California purposes and who received compensation or executes a contract for services performed for that service-recipient within or without the state."
  — Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1088.8(b)(2) (California Legislative Information text), California Unemployment Insurance Code, definition of "service-provider" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=UIC&sectionNum=1088.8)
  "Each service-recipient shall report all of the following information to the department, within 20 days of the earlier of first making payments that in the aggregate equal or exceed six hundred dollars ($600) in any year to a service-provider, or entering into a contract or contracts with a service-provider providing for payments that in the aggregate equal or exceed six hundred dollars ($600) in any year:"
  — Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1088.8(c) (California Legislative Information text), California Unemployment Insurance Code, the $600 aggregate-payment reporting trigger and 20-day deadline (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=UIC&sectionNum=1088.8)
  "The full name, address, and social security number of the service-provider."
  — Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1088.8(c)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California Unemployment Insurance Code, required service-provider information (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=UIC&sectionNum=1088.8)
  Known gap: This is California law, used as evidence of what California requires — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any specific employer's situation. This information sheet is informational only: it does not itself file a new-hire report with the California Employment Development Department or any other agency, and it does not itself fulfill any employer's reporting duty. This is a real, and easy to miss, feature of California's program: it is not limited to common-law employees the way the federal underlying statute, 42 U.S.C. § 653a, is. All four citations below are to different subdivisions of the same statutory section, Unemployment Insurance Code § 1088.8 — subdivisions (a) and (b)(2) (who is covered) and subdivision (c) and its paragraph (1) (the trigger and required content) — and are treated as one source, not independent. This clause does not summarize § 1088.8(c)'s remaining required-content items (the service-recipient's own identifying information, the contract date, and the contract's dollar amount), nor § 1088.8(d)'s retention period for the department, nor § 1088.8(f)'s limits on how the department may use information collected under this section. Section 1088.8(e) sets the same $24/$490 penalty structure described in this information sheet's penalties clause, applied here to a service-recipient's own failure to comply with subdivision (c).

ACKNOWLEDGMENT
The following information reflects what a completed new hire report for Jordan Alex Lee would need to contain under Unemployment Insurance Code § 1088.5(d)(4):

Employee name: Jordan Alex Lee
Employee address: 500 Market St, San Francisco, CA 94105
First date of work: October 1, 2026
Employer name: Acme Corp

Section 1088.5(d)(4)(A) also requires the employee's Social Security number as part of the actual report. This information sheet does not include a fill-in field for it: no full Social Security number is recorded on this document. Consistent with § 1088.5(d)(5), an employer may report that number directly from Jordan Alex Lee's completed Form W-4 or the equivalent form used to make the actual report to the Employment Development Department, rather than copying it onto a separate information sheet like this one.

Please sign below to acknowledge that you received this information sheet.

Employee: Jordan Alex Lee
Signature: _______________  Date: _______________

On behalf of Acme Corp:
Signature: _______________  Date: _______________

expectedJSON.body: California law authorizes the Employment Development Department to assess a penalty of $24 for each failure to report the hiring of an employee as required and within the time required, unless the failure is due to good cause; the penalty rises to $490 if the failure results from a conspiracy between the employer and the employee not to supply the required report, or to supply a false or incomplete one. These amounts are not California's own invention set independent of federal law: the federal statute underlying this program caps what a state may set its new-hire-reporting civil penalty at — no more than $25 per failure, or $500 for a conspiracy — and California's own codified penalty amounts sit at or under that federal ceiling.

citations.case: Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1088.5(e) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Unemployment Insurance Code, the codified penalty amounts
citations.quote: For each failure to report the hiring of an employee, as required and within the time required by this section, unless the failure is due to good cause, the department may assess a penalty of twenty-four dollars ($24), or four hundred ninety dollars ($490) if the failure is the result of conspiracy between the employer and employee not to supply the required report or to supply a false or incomplete report.

citations.cite: Federal statute, the ceiling on a state's new-hire-reporting civil penalty
citations.quote: The State shall have the option to set a State civil money penalty which shall not exceed— (1) $25 per failure to meet the requirements of this section with respect to a newly hired employee ; or (2) $500 if, under State law, the failure is the result of a conspiracy between the employer and the employee to not supply the required report or to supply a false or incomplete report.

expectedJSON.body: California law imposes a second, independent reporting duty distinct from the employee new-hire reporting duty described above: a "service-recipient" — defined to include an individual, corporation, association, or partnership doing business in the state — that makes or is required to make an information return to the IRS under Internal Revenue Code § 6041A for payments to a "service-provider" (an individual who is not its employee for California purposes) must also report specified information to the Employment Development Department. That duty is triggered within 20 days of the earlier of two events: the service-recipient's aggregate payments to that service-provider first reaching $600 in a calendar year, or the service-recipient entering into a contract or contracts with that service-provider providing for aggregate payments of $600 or more in a calendar year. The required report includes the service-provider's full name, address, and Social Security number, among other identifying information.

citations.case: Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1088.8(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Unemployment Insurance Code, the independent-contractor reporting trigger (IRC § 6041A)
citations.quote: Effective January 1, 2001, any service-recipient, as defined in subdivision (b), who makes or is required to make a return to the Internal Revenue Service, in accordance with subdivision (a) of Section 6041A of the Internal Revenue Code (relating to payments made to a service-provider as compensation for services) shall file with the department information as required under subdivision (c).

citations.case: Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1088.8(b)(2) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Unemployment Insurance Code, definition of "service-provider"
citations.quote: “Service-provider” means an individual who is not an employee of the service-recipient for California purposes and who received compensation or executes a contract for services performed for that service-recipient within or without the state.

citations.case: Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1088.8(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Unemployment Insurance Code, the $600 aggregate-payment reporting trigger and 20-day deadline
citations.quote: Each service-recipient shall report all of the following information to the department, within 20 days of the earlier of first making payments that in the aggregate equal or exceed six hundred dollars ($600) in any year to a service-provider, or entering into a contract or contracts with a service-provider providing for payments that in the aggregate equal or exceed six hundred dollars ($600) in any year:

citations.case: Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1088.8(c)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Unemployment Insurance Code, required service-provider information
citations.quote: The full name, address, and social security number of the service-provider.

The following information reflects what a completed new hire report for Jordan Alex Lee would need to contain under Unemployment Insurance Code § 1088.5(d)(4):

Employee name: Jordan Alex Lee
Employee address: 500 Market St, San Francisco, CA 94105
First date of work: October 1, 2026
Employer name: Acme Corp

Section 1088.5(d)(4)(A) also requires the employee's Social Security number as part of the actual report. This information sheet does not include a fill-in field for it: no full Social Security number is recorded on this document. Consistent with § 1088.5(d)(5), an employer may report that number directly from Jordan Alex Lee's completed Form W-4 or the equivalent form used to make the actual report to the Employment Development Department, rather than copying it onto a separate information sheet like this one.
